title: Match Substring After Replacement
statement:
You get a string `s`, a shorter-or-equal string `sub`, and a list `mappings` of pairs `[old, new]`. A pair lets you turn any occurrence of the character `old` in `sub` into the character `new`; pairs work in that direction only and may be used at as many positions as you like.

Every position of `sub` may be changed at most once, so replacements never chain: a character that came from a replacement stays as it is. Characters are case sensitive.

Return `true` if some set of such changes (possibly none) makes `sub` appear in `s` as a block of consecutive characters, and `false` otherwise.
constraints: s and sub contain only uppercase letters, lowercase letters and digits
old_i and new_i are uppercase letters, lowercase letters or digits
signature: boolean matchReplacement(String s, String sub, char[][] mappings)
notes:
## Intuition

`sub` has to line up with some window of `s` of the same length, so we can simply try every window, as the brute force does. The only question per position is whether `sub`'s character can show up as the character of `s` there: either they are already equal, or one pair `[want, have]` turns one into the other. Since replacements never chain, a single lookup answers that. Storing the pairs in a map from `old` to the set of its `new` characters makes the lookup constant time.

## Approach

1. Build `canBecome`: for each pair `[from, to]`, add `to` to the set stored under `from`.
2. For every `start` where a window of length `sub.length` fits in `s`, assume `matches`.
3. Walk `j` along `sub`, comparing `want = sub[j]` with `have = s[start + j]`.
4. If they differ and `want` cannot become `have`, this window fails; stop scanning it.
5. If a window survives every position, return `true`. If none does, return `false`.

## Example 1, step by step

`canBecome` is `e -> {3}`, `t -> {7, 8}`. Windows of length 4 in `"fool3e7bar"`: `"fool"` fails at once (`l` vs `f`), `"ool3"` and `"ol3e"` fail on their first letter too. At `start = 3` the window is `"l3e7"`: `l = l`, `e -> 3` is allowed, `e = e`, `t -> 7` is allowed, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k + n · m) for `k` mappings, `n = s.length`, `m = sub.length`: each window checks up to `m` positions with constant-time lookups.
- Space: O(k) for the map of allowed replacements.

## Pitfalls

- Mappings are one way: `["o", "0"]` lets `sub`'s `o` match `s`'s `0`, never the reverse.
- Do not chain pairs: `a -> b` and `b -> c` do not let `a` match `c`.
- One character may have several targets (`t -> 7` and `t -> 8`), so store a set, not a single value.
- Letters are case sensitive, so `"F"` and `"f"` differ unless a pair says otherwise.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `canBecome` | map from a character of `sub` to the set of characters it may turn into |
| `start` | index in `s` where the current window begins |
| `matches` | whether the current window still fits so far |
| `j` | position inside `sub` |
| `want`, `have` | the characters of `sub` and of `s` being compared |
